summary: Documents an existing, widely used protocol and common implementation: BSD rlogin. It is informational and not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: BSD rlogin lets a user operate a remote Unix host through a terminal connection. This memo describes session setup, terminal controls and the security risks of password-free trusted-host login.

questions: how does rlogin window size change work
why is rlogin trusted host login risky
subtitle: How BSD rlogin opens a remote terminal session over TCP and handles terminal controls.

tldr.problem: Unix users wanted a remote terminal that carried more Unix terminal behavior than Telnet and could, on some hosts, avoid password entry from trusted hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The client connects to TCP port 513, sends four null-terminated strings, and exchanges terminal data and control messages with the server.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents an existing protocol, not an Internet standard, and warns that trusted-host password bypass weakens security.

today: RFC 1282 is an Informational memo that documents an existing protocol rather than specifying an Internet standard. It obsoletes RFC 1258.

sections.title: What BSD Rlogin Provides
sections.content:
The rlogin facility provides a remote-echoed, locally flow-controlled virtual terminal. The memo says it was widely used between Unix hosts because it carries more Unix terminal behavior than Telnet and could be configured on some hosts to skip password entry for connections from trusted hosts.

Rlogin uses TCP, connects to port 513, and assumes an eight-bit transparent stream. RFC 1282 documents an existing protocol and implementation; it does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Rlogin lets someone use a remote computer through a terminal. The connection uses TCP and the server listens on port 513.

sections.title: Opening a Session
sections.content:
After the TCP connection opens, the client sends four null-terminated strings: an empty string, the client username, the server username, and the terminal type and speed. The server returns a zero byte to indicate that it has received them and entered data-transfer mode.

Window-size negotiation may follow. When the TCP connection closes, the side that notices should restore terminal modes, notify the user or processes, and then close the connection in the other direction.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends two usernames and information about its terminal. The server replies with a zero byte when it is ready to exchange terminal data.

sections.title: Terminal Controls and Window Size
sections.content:
In cooked mode, the client intercepts START and STOP characters to pause or resume remote output. In raw mode, those characters are sent to the server as ordinary data. The server can send control bytes using TCP urgent data: 02 discards buffered output, 10 switches to raw mode, 20 resumes local START and STOP handling, and 80 asks for the current window size.

If the server accepts window changes, the client sends a 12-byte sequence with a magic cookie, two lowercase s bytes, and four 16-bit dimensions: character rows, characters per row, and pixel width and height. The client also has an escape character, customarily tilde, with special behavior at the beginning of a line.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server use control messages to manage terminal output. The client can also report the terminal's current size after a resize.

sections.title: Risks of Trusted-Host Login
sections.content:
The memo warns that password-free login from trusted hosts weakens security and has been exploited. If several systems trust one another, compromise of one can expose the others. The memo describes limiting password bypass to one workstation as a possible compromise.

A trusted host name can be spoofed if an organization's domain name server or network is compromised. A trusted-login file that other users can write can also be changed. Secure authentication extensions such as Kerberos can reduce the risk while preserving password-entry convenience.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping passwords can let an attacker move from one compromised system to others that trust it. The memo recommends understanding this risk and notes that secure authentication extensions can reduce it.
